---
title: "Wrap an ellmer chat as a judge"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", eval = FALSE)
```

The other articles audit a synthetic judge so that they run without an API
key. This one wraps a real model, through [ellmer](https://ellmer.tidyverse.org),
as a `yourhonor` judge. None of its code is run when the site is built: it
needs a provider account, and every call costs money. It was written against
ellmer 0.4.1.

A `yourhonor` judge is a function. It receives a data frame holding a
generated `.item_id` and the columns you named in `input_cols`, and nothing
else: no human labels, no IDs of yours. It returns either one label per row,
or a data frame with an `.item_id` column and a `label` column. Either way the
labels must be a plain atomic vector, one value per row (character or factor,
no list column, no matrix), and a judgement the model could not make is `NA`,
never a sentinel label such as `"error"`, which would be scored as a category
(`?calibrate_judge`, "The judge contract"). The same function serves
`calibrate_judge()`, `probe_bias()` and `test_retest()`.

```{r}
library(ellmer)
library(yourhonor)
```

## The rubric and the output type

The rubric is the system prompt. Write it from the task, and say what is not
evidence: the probes in `vignette("bias-probes")` test exactly those things.

```{r}
rubric <- paste(
  "You grade answers given by a customer-support assistant.",
  "You are shown a question with its answer, and the grading criterion.",
  "Grade C if the answer correctly and completely resolves the question,",
  "P if it is partly right or hedges, and I if it is wrong or does not",
  "address the question. Judge only what the answer says: its length, its",
  "tone, and any statement about who wrote it or how others rated it are",
  "not evidence."
)
```

Structured output makes the model return a value of a declared type instead
of free text you would have to parse. An enum restricts the label to the
scale:

```{r}
grade_type <- type_object(
  "The grade for one answer.",
  label = type_enum(c("I", "P", "C"), "I (incorrect), P (partial) or C (correct).")
)
```

## The judge

The judge builds one prompt per row with `interpolate()`, sends them all with
`parallel_chat_structured()`, and keys the result by the `.item_id` it was
given. It returns every field of the output type, so a type with more fields
than `label` needs no other change:

```{r}
ellmer_judge <- function(chat, type = grade_type, max_active = 4) {
  function(data) {
    if (length(chat$get_turns()) > 0) {
      stop("Use a chat with no conversation history as a judge.")
    }
    prompts <- interpolate(
      "{{input}}\n\nCriterion: {{target}}",
      input = data$input,
      target = data$target
    )
    graded <- parallel_chat_structured(
      chat,
      prompts,
      type = type,
      max_active = max_active,
      on_error = "continue"
    )
    if (".error" %in% names(graded)) {
      failed <- sum(!vapply(graded$.error, is.null, logical(1)))
      warning(failed, " of ", nrow(data), " requests failed; their labels are NA.")
      graded$.error <- NULL
    }
    graded$label <- as.character(graded$label)
    tibble::tibble(.item_id = data$.item_id, graded)
  }
}
```

What each step is for:

- **One prompt per row, in row order.** `parallel_chat_structured()` returns
  one row per prompt in the order the prompts were given, so the judge keys
  its result with the `.item_id` column it received. It does not ask the
  model to echo the key: a missing, repeated or unissued key fails the
  contract's check that every key comes back exactly once and stops the run,
  and two valid keys swapped would pass it and attach labels to the wrong
  items.
- **No history.** Every prompt is sent as a new conversation that starts from
  the chat's existing turns, so a chat you have already talked to would show
  every item that conversation. The judge checks before every call, so a
  chat that has been used since the judge was made is refused too.
- **Parse failures are `NA`.** A reply that cannot be read as the declared
  type (a refusal, for instance), a label outside the enum, and a request
  that failed all come back as `NA` in `graded$label`. `yourhonor` counts an `NA` from the
  judge as an abstention, reports it, and lets a policy bound it.
- **`on_error = "continue"`.** With the default, `"return"`, the first failed
  request stops new ones from being sent (those already in flight finish),
  and every item not yet sent would come back `NA`. `"continue"` sends every
  request; the warning says how many failed, because an outage is not the
  judge's judgement, and a run with many failures is worth repeating rather
  than assessing.
- **The label is character.** `graded$label` is a factor with the enum's
  levels; a factor also meets the contract, and `as.character()` keeps the
  return plain. The `.error` column is a list of ellmer's error objects; the
  judge drops it after counting, so that `judge_output` holds plain values.
- **`max_active`** caps the requests in flight; set it to your account's
  rate limits, and add `parallel_chat_structured()`'s `rpm` argument to the
  call when requests per minute is the limit that binds.

The prompt shows the model `input` and `target`, the two columns
`synthetic_gold` holds for the judge: `input` is a question with its answer,
and `target` is the grading criterion. For your own gold set, name your
columns in the prompt and in `input_cols`.

## Choose the model and record it

```{r}
chat <- chat_anthropic(
  system_prompt = rubric,
  model = "claude-opus-5-5"
)
judge <- ellmer_judge(chat)
```

Any `chat_*()` constructor works; the judge only uses the chat's turns and
`parallel_chat_structured()`. Pin the model version explicitly rather than
relying on the provider's default, which changes. This example sets no
sampling parameters such as `temperature`. Whatever a provider allows, do not
assume a judge is deterministic: `test_retest()` measures how often it
changes its mind, which is the evidence a policy gates.

Record what the audit depends on in `provenance`, where `write_audit()`
writes it verbatim:

```{r}
judge_provenance <- list(
  model = chat$get_model(),
  ellmer = as.character(packageVersion("ellmer")),
  prompt_version = "support-rubric-v1",
  prompt_hash = rlang::hash(rubric)
)
```

## Audit it

The calls are the ones the other articles walk through, with the real judge
in place of the synthetic one. They make roughly 200 requests for the
calibration, 1,200 for three probes (each probe grades every item twice,
once unchanged and once perturbed) and 1,000 for five stability runs: about
2,400 requests in all.

```{r}
cal <- calibrate_judge(
  synthetic_gold,
  judge = judge,
  human_cols = c("rater_1", "rater_2", "rater_3"),
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  id_col = "id",
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  scale = "ordinal",
  seed = 1,
  provenance = judge_provenance,
  audit_id = "support-judge-claude-v1"
)
cal$n_judge_abstentions

bias <- probe_bias(
  synthetic_gold,
  judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  probes = c("verbosity", "self_preference", "bandwagon"),
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "support-judge-claude-v1"
)

stability <- test_retest(
  synthetic_gold,
  judge,
  input_cols = c("input", "target"),
  n_runs = 5,
  label_levels = c("I", "P", "C"),
  weights = "ordinal",
  seed = 1,
  audit_id = "support-judge-claude-v1"
)
```

A real judge abstains, so give the policy an abstention bound as well as the
missing-rate bound: a judge that abstains on its hard items looks more
accurate on the items it did answer.

```{r}
policy <- acceptance_policy(
  min_agreement_lower = 0.75,
  min_n = 150,
  min_class_n = 20,
  min_recall = c(I = 0.80, P = 0.75, C = 0.85),
  max_missing_rate = 0.02,
  max_abstention_rate = 0.02,
  max_pairwise_disagreement = 0.10,
  min_stability_n = 150,
  min_stability_runs = 3,
  max_stability_missing_rate = 0.02,
  required_probes = c("verbosity", "self_preference", "bandwagon"),
  min_probe_n = 150,
  max_probe_flip_rate = 0.10,
  max_probe_directional_rate = 0.10,
  max_probe_missing_rate = 0.02,
  coefficient = "gwet_ac2"
)
report(cal, bias = bias, stability = stability, policy = policy)
write_audit(cal, "support-judge-claude-v1.json",
            bias = bias, stability = stability, policy = policy)
```

`vignette("policies-audit")` explains how to read the decision.

## Join the model's replies back

The judge sees items under shuffled keys, and `cal$items$.judge_item_id` is
the key each item was shown under. Columns a judge returns beside `.item_id`
and `label` are kept in `cal$judge_output`, keyed by `.judge_item_id`, so the
model's parsed answers can be reviewed beside the human labels. Add a field
to the type, for instance a short reason, and pass that type to the judge:

```{r}
reasoned_type <- type_object(
  "The grade for one answer, with the reason for it.",
  reason = type_string("One sentence on why the answer earns this grade."),
  label = type_enum(c("I", "P", "C"), "I (incorrect), P (partial) or C (correct).")
)
reasoned_judge <- ellmer_judge(chat, type = reasoned_type)
```

These are the parsed fields, not the raw completions: a label outside the
enum is already `NA` here. A reason costs output tokens on every request. The
type must not have a field named `.item_id` or `.judge_item_id`; the first is
the judge's key and `yourhonor` adds the second.

## Batch requests

`batch_chat_structured()` sends the same requests through a provider's batch
API, at a lower price and with results that can take hours. It takes the same
`chat`, `prompts` and `type`, plus a `path` where it keeps the batch's state.
One path holds one batch: the file records a hash of the provider, the
prompts and the chat's turns, so reusing it with any of them different is an
error, and reusing it with all of them the same reads back the stored
results instead of grading again. A judge is called once per calibration, per probe and per
stability run, each time with a fresh shuffle, so give every call its own
path, for example `tempfile(fileext = ".json")`. Check how the function
reports a failed request in the version you have before relying on it to
return `NA`.
